analysis.one_liner: Requires anti-entrapment drain covers on all public pools and funds drowning-prevention education.
analysis.headline: The bill passed the Senate Commerce Committee with bipartisan support but never got a Senate floor vote; the same requirements became law anyway that December inside an energy bill the president signed.
analysis.plain_summary: Drowning is a leading cause of death for young children, and powerful pool drains can trap swimmers underwater. This bill would require every public pool and spa in the country to use drain covers and systems that meet a federal anti-entrapment safety standard, and require new drain covers sold anywhere to meet that standard. It would also give small grants to states that pass their own pool safety laws and pay the Consumer Product Safety Commission to run a public education campaign on drowning prevention.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and families who use public pools — at hotels, apartment complexes, community pools, and military bases — where a defective or missing drain cover can trap a swimmer underwater. Pool safety also improves at home in states that take the federal grants and pass their own barrier and entrapment-prevention laws.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every public pool and spa in the United States — including hotel, apartment, club, and federally operated pools — to be equipped with anti-entrapment drain devices meeting the ASME/ANSI A112.19.8 standard, enforceable under the Consumer Product Safety Act [S3][S4].
Requires every drain cover manufactured or sold in the U.S. to conform to the federal entrapment-protection standard, so safe covers cannot be undercut by cheaper unsafe ones [S2][S3].
Authorizes $2 million a year in grants to states that enact minimum pool safety laws, including fencing to keep unsupervised children out of residential pools [S3][S4].
Directs the CPSC to run a public education campaign on drowning and entrapment prevention, funded at up to $5 million a year [S4].
Congress found that drowning is the second leading cause of injury-related death among children 1 to 14, with 761 children 14 and under dying by unintentional drowning in 2004 [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Public pool operators — hotels, apartment complexes, clubs, community pools, and military and federal facilities — must buy and install compliant drain covers and entrapment-prevention systems. Pool equipment makers and service companies gain the work. Taxpayers fund the small grant and education programs.

drawbacks.text: The public pool mandate is a compliance cost for thousands of operators — hotels, apartment buildings, and community pools must retrofit drains and covers within a year of enactment [S3][S4].

The federal requirements cover public pools but not private backyard pools, except indirectly through voluntary state grants; Congress's own findings say barriers and fencing substantially reduce residential drownings, meaning the biggest residential risk is addressed only if states opt in [S4].
The grant program is small — $2 million a year — and states only qualify if they pass new laws covering all pools, so funding could reach few states [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost is modest and targeted: one-time retrofit expenses for pool operators against a federal standard aimed at preventing childhood drownings and entrapment deaths. The main design gap is that the strongest protections for private backyard pools depend on states enacting their own laws to win grants, and the grant money is small.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Commerce Committee approved it with bipartisan support in September 2007 and it sat on the Senate calendar, but it never came to the floor before Congress ended — yet the same pool safety law was enacted anyway that December as a title of the Energy Independence and Security Act, which President Bush signed.

narrative.text: Sen. Mark Pryor introduced the bill on July 11, 2007 with an evenly bipartisan group of 10 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the Commerce Committee [S4][S6].

The committee ordered the bill reported favorably with amendments on July 19, 2007, and reported it on September 20 with a written report; it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders [S6].
No floor vote ever occurred; the bill remained on the calendar until the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S6].
The reported bill would have made anti-entrapment drain covers mandatory on all public pools and created state grant and CPSC education programs [S3][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Swimmers and their families came out ahead: despite this bill itself dying on the Senate calendar, the identical Virginia Graeme Baker Pool and Spa Safety Act became law in December 2007 as part of the Energy Independence and Security Act, so the public got the protections without this chamber-level fight. Public pool operators who would have borne retrofit costs gained only a delay.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Swimmers — the same law passed anyway

for.name: Sen. Mark Pryor
for.what_they_did: Introduced S. 1771 and assembled 10 original cosponsors from both parties

for.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
for.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Sen. Daniel Inouye
for.what_they_did: Ordered the bill reported favorably with amendments on July 19, 2007 and reported it September 20, 2007 with Report No. 110-182

for.name: President George W. Bush
for.what_they_did: Signed the Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007, which contained the Virginia Graeme Baker Pool and Spa Safety Act as one of its titles

for.name: Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz
for.role: U.S. Representative (FL), House champion of the bill
for.what_they_did: Led the push in the House for the Virginia Graeme Baker Act, which she named for a young constituent who died in a hot tub drain entrapment

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Democrat with an evenly split cosponsor list (6 Democrats, 5 Republicans), and no opposition appears anywhere in the record — it died from inaction, not votes.

industries.industry: Pool equipment manufacturers (drain covers, safety vacuum release systems)
industries.note: Federal rules make compliant anti-entrapment drain covers and systems mandatory equipment for every public pool, creating guaranteed demand. The product's purpose — preventing children from being trapped underwater — runs directly alongside the public's interest.

industries.industry: Public pool operators (hotels, apartment complexes, clubs, community and federal pools)
industries.note: Operators must retrofit drains and install compliant covers within a year or face enforcement under the Consumer Product Safety Act. The cost falls on them while the safety benefit goes to the public.

industries.industry: Pool construction, service, and installation companies
industries.note: The bill funds education programs aimed at these companies and generates retrofit work as pools upgrade to the new standard.
